chapter.title: This or That: Commonly Confused Words
chapter.description: Master frequently confused word pairs in English with clear, individual comparisons, simple explanations, and distinct examples for both words.

sections.title: Good vs. Well
sections.explanation: 'Good' is an adjective that describes a person, place, or thing. 'Well' is an adverb that describes how an action is performed (or refers to physical health).

exercises.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: You did a good job on that presentation.
You did a well job on that presentation.
exercises.answer: You did a good job on that presentation.
exercises.explanation: 'Good' is an adjective modifying the noun 'job'.

exercises.question: Choose the correct sentence.
exercises.explanation: 'Well' is an adverb describing the action verb 'sings'.

exercises.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I do not feel good today, so I am staying home.
I do not feel well today, so I am staying home.
exercises.answer: I do not feel well today, so I am staying home.

exercises.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The pasta sauce smells really good.
The pasta sauce smells really well.
exercises.answer: The pasta sauce smells really good.
exercises.explanation: Sense verbs like 'smells' take the adjective 'good'.

exercises.question: Choose the correct sentence.
exercises.explanation: 'Well' modifies how he performs the verb 'speaks'.

sections.title: Bad vs. Badly
sections.explanation: 'Bad' is an adjective that describes a noun or follows a linking verb like 'feel' or 'smell'. 'Badly' is an adverb that describes how an action verb is performed.

examples.bad: I feel bad about missing your party.
examples.badly: The team played badly in the first half.

exercises.question: I feel ________ about forgetting your birthday.
exercises.explanation: Linking verbs of emotion ('feel') take the adjective 'bad'.

exercises.question: The engine was damaged ________ in the accident.
exercises.explanation: 'Badly' is an adverb describing the extent of the damage.

exercises.question: That milk smells ________.
He performed ________ during the audition.
It is a ________ situation for everyone involved.

sections.title: I vs. Me
sections.explanation: Use 'I' when you are the subject doing the action. Use 'me' when you are the object receiving the action or after a preposition.

examples.i: Sarah and I went to the market.
examples.me: The teacher called Sarah and me.

exercises.question: Sarah and ________ went to the movies.
exercises.explanation: 'I' is part of the compound subject of the sentence.

exercises.question: The teacher gave the books to Mark and ________.
exercises.explanation: 'Me' is the object of the preposition 'to'.

exercises.question: Between you and ________, this project is exhausting.
exercises.explanation: The preposition 'between' requires the object pronoun 'me'.

exercises.question: He is taller than ________.
exercises.explanation: 'Than I' is short for 'than I am'.

exercises.question: They invited my brother and ________ to the party.
exercises.explanation: 'Me' is a direct object of the verb 'invited'.

sections.title: Lie vs. Lay
sections.explanation: Use 'lie' to mean resting or reclining yourself (no object needed). Use 'lay' to mean placing an object down (requires an object).

examples.lie: I need to lie down on the couch.
examples.lay: Please lay the book on the table.

exercises.question: Please ____ the carpet flat on the floor.
I am going to ____ down for an hour.
exercises.explanation: 'Lie' is intransitive and takes no direct object.

exercises.question: Yesterday, he ____ on the couch all afternoon.
exercises.explanation: 'Lay' is the past tense of 'lie' (to recline).

exercises.question: She ____ her keys on the counter this morning.
exercises.explanation: 'Laid' is the past tense of 'lay' (to place something down).

exercises.question: The dog has ____ in the sun all morning.
exercises.explanation: 'Lain' is the past participle of the intransitive verb 'lie'.

exercises.question: The hens have ____ three eggs today.
exercises.explanation: 'Laid' is the past participle of 'lay' (to produce/place eggs).

exercises.question: ____ the baby in her crib carefully.
The papers were ____ on the table when I arrived.
He told me to ____ the book down.
The patient was ____ on the examination table.
exercises.explanation: 'Lying' is used because the patient is reclining (no direct object).

sections.title: Rise vs. Raise
sections.explanation: Use 'rise' when something moves upward on its own (no object needed). Use 'raise' when someone lifts something else up (requires an object).

examples.rise: The sun rises in the east.
examples.raise: Please raise your hand to ask a question.

exercises.question: The sun will ____ at 6:00 AM tomorrow.
exercises.explanation: 'Rise' is an intransitive verb (no direct object).

exercises.question: The company decided to ____ prices next month.
exercises.explanation: 'Raise' is a transitive verb taking the direct object ('prices').

exercises.question: Prices tend to ____ during inflation.
exercises.explanation: 'Rise' is an intransitive action (goes up by itself).

exercises.question: Please ____ your hand if you have a question.

sections.title: Into vs. In to
sections.explanation: Use 'into' as a single preposition to show movement toward the inside of something. Use 'in to' when 'in' is part of a verb phrase and 'to' belongs to the next word.

examples.in-to: He turned his assignment in to the teacher.

exercises.question: She walked ________ the store to buy bread.
Please come ________ see me tomorrow.
exercises.explanation: 'In' is part of the verb phrase 'come in', followed by the infinitive 'to'.

exercises.question: He dropped his phone ________ the water.
Turn your tests ________ the teacher when finished.
The caterpillar transformed ________ a butterfly.

sections.title: Onto vs. On to
sections.explanation: Use 'onto' as a single preposition to show movement moving on top of a surface. Use 'on to' when 'on' is part of a verb phrase or leads to an infinitive.

examples.onto: The cat jumped onto the roof.
examples.on-to: We decided to hold on to the railing.

exercises.question: The cat jumped ________ the counter.
Hold ________ your hat in this wind!
exercises.explanation: 'On' belongs to the phrasal verb 'hold on'.

exercises.question: We moved ________ the next topic on the agenda.
He stepped out ________ the balcony.
Log ________ the website to register.

sections.title: Look vs. See vs. Watch
sections.explanation: Use 'see' when a sound or image comes into your sight automatically. Use 'look (at)' when you direct your eyes on purpose. Use 'watch' when you pay attention to something in motion over time.

examples.see: I can see the mountains from here.
examples.watch: We watch a movie every Friday.

exercises.question: Can you ____ that bird in the tree?
____ at the blackboard, please.
Did you ____ the football match last night?
exercises.explanation: 'Watch' means paying attention to an event over time.

exercises.question: I turned around and ____ him standing there.
She loves to ____ movies on weekends.

sections.title: Hear vs. Listen
sections.explanation: Use 'hear' when sounds enter your ears naturally without effort. Use 'listen (to)' when you pay active attention to a sound on purpose.

examples.hear: Did you hear that noise outside?
examples.listen: I listen to music while working.

exercises.question: Speak up, I can't ____ you very well.
Are you ____ to the radio right now?
Suddenly, we ____ a loud explosion.
You should ____ to your doctor's advice.
Did you ____ what she said?

sections.title: Lose vs. Loose
sections.explanation: Use 'lose' (verb) when you misplace something or suffer defeat. Use 'loose' (adjective) when something is not tight or fixed securely.

exercises.question: Be careful not to ________ your passport.
exercises.explanation: 'Lose' is a verb meaning to misplace.

exercises.question: This knot is ________; it might come undone.
If we ________ this game, we are out of the tournament.
She wears ________ clothing in the summer.
Did you ________ your keys again?

sections.title: Bring vs. Take
sections.explanation: Use 'bring' when moving something toward the speaker/listener location. Use 'take' when carrying something away from the current location.

examples.bring: Please bring me a cup of coffee.
examples.take: Don't forget to take your umbrella when you leave.

exercises.question: Please ________ your homework to class tomorrow.
Remember to ________ out the trash when you leave.
exercises.explanation: 'Take' means movement away from a place.

exercises.question: Can you ________ me a glass of water?
exercises.explanation: 'Bring' means carry toward the person asking.

exercises.question: He will ________ his dog to the vet later.
exercises.explanation: 'Take' means moving away to another destination.

exercises.question: ________ some snacks when you come over!
exercises.explanation: 'Bring' indicates bringing items to the host's place.

sections.title: Say vs. Tell
sections.explanation: Use 'say' to express words directly (often followed by 'to someone'). Use 'tell' when giving information directly to a person (requires a personal object like me, him, us).

exercises.question: What did he ____ to you?
Don't ____ anyone my secret!
She ____ goodbye and left the room.
exercises.explanation: Expressing words without a personal object uses 'said'.
